2024_018_2_a_24680_troy_school_district_.paragraph: Plante & Moran, PLLC's report to the Troy School District Board of Education on the audit of the basic financial statements for the year ended June 30, 2024, dated October 28, 2024 and presented at the November 12, 2024 meeting. The letter is organized into Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), and Informational Items (pages 7-19), and reports no disagreements with management, no significant difficulties, and all identified misstatements corrected. The single recommendation is that the Food Service Fund balance continues to exceed the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures, requiring continued monitoring of the spenddown plan entered into with the Michigan Department of Education.
2024_018_2_a_24680_troy_school_district_.page:
**Engagement and issuance**
Auditor: Plante & Moran, PLLC, signed by Chris Geck, CPA (Partner) and Michael Walsh, CPA (Senior Manager). Audit of the basic financial statements of Troy School District for the year ended June 30, 2024; audit report and this letter both dated October 28, 2024. Engagement letter dated June 17, 2024; planning meeting August 27, 2024; management representation letter dated October 28, 2024. The firm thanked Mr. Dan Trudel, Mr. Aurel Malutan, and the business office. A separate October 28, 2024 letter covers internal control over financial reporting and compliance testing under Government Auditing Standards.

**Results of the audit (pages 1-4)**
No new accounting policies adopted and no change in application of existing policies during 2024; no transactions lacking authoritative guidance; no transactions recognized in a different period than when they occurred; disclosures neutral, consistent, and clear. No significant difficulties, no disagreements with management, and management corrected all accumulated misstatements. No consultations with other independent accountants.

**Most sensitive estimates**

| Estimate (GASB 68 / 75) | District share at June 30, 2024 |
| --- | --- |
| MPSERS net pension liability | $288.9 million |
| OPEB net asset | $4.9 million |

**Other recommendations and observations (pages 5-6)**
Food Service Fund - Fund Balance: the fund balance continues to exceed the USDA maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures; the District should continue to monitor its spenddown plan entered into with the Michigan Department of Education.

**School funding items (pages 7-19)**
2023/2024 state funding raised the target foundation allowance by $458 per pupil to $9,608 (a 5 percent increase), with cyber schools held at $9,150; the blended pupil count remained 90 percent October 2023 and 10 percent February 2023, with Section 29 support for declining-enrollment districts. Special education funding moved fully to Section 51 as a categorical rather than Section 20. The MPSERS contribution rate rose to 48 percent of payroll from 45 percent, with the District's net cost rising from 28 percent to approximately 31 percent. For 2024/2025 the target foundation allowance stays at $9,608 with no increase; retirement changes through Section 147 and new categorical 147a4 free up about $400 per pupil, with 147a4 representing approximately 5.75 percent of MPSERS-related payroll. The statewide historical OPEB UAAL is about $669 million, of which the School Aid Bill redirects $598 million back to districts. At-risk funding is now over $1 billion, and ARP ESSER III sunset September 30, 2024. At September 30, 2023 the statewide MPSERS net pension liability was approximately $32.4 billion, down about 15 percent from $37.9 billion, with a net OPEB asset of approximately $566 million.

**District-specific figures**

| Item | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Section 30d state school meals funding, 2023/2024 | $3,676,677 |
| General Fund revenue over expenditures, 2023/2024 | approximately $4.2 million |
| General Fund fund balance at June 30, 2024 | approximately $36.8 million |
| District fund balance percentage | 19.21 percent (about 10 weeks of operation) |
| Statewide average at June 30, 2023 | approximately 21.86 percent (about 11 weeks) |
| Arbitrage liability reported at June 30, 2024 | $3,693,631 |

**Upcoming pronouncements and compliance changes**
GASB 101 (Compensated Absences) and GASB 102 (Certain Risk Disclosures) are effective for the year ending June 30, 2025; GASB 103 (Financial Reporting Model Improvements) for June 30, 2026. Sinking fund legislation effective August 6, 2023 allows millages approved after May 7, 2023 to fund student transportation vehicles and related maintenance. Treasury Numbered Letter 2023-1 supersedes Bulletin 7 and Numbered Letter 2004-4 beginning with the June 30, 2024 reporting period. OMB's April 2024 Uniform Guidance revisions raise the single audit and Type A thresholds from $750,000 to $1 million and the equipment capitalization threshold from $5,000 to $10,000. Advisory items close the letter on grants management risk assessment, cyber threats, operations and controls review, IT assessment, and data analytics.
2024_018_2_a_24680_troy_school_district_.verbose:
Report to the Board of Education of Troy School District on the audit of the basic financial statements as of and for the year ended June 30, 2024, issued by Plante & Moran, PLLC and dated October 28, 2024, presented on the November 12, 2024 agenda. Sections and page references: Results of the Audit (1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (5-6), Informational Items (7-19). The firm thanked Mr. Dan Trudel, Mr. Aurel Malutan, and the entire business office. Signed by Chris Geck, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Senior Manager.

RESULTS OF THE AUDIT. Under the engagement letter dated June 17, 2024, the auditor's responsibility is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements prepared by management with board oversight are fairly presented in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles. The audit was also conducted under Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States; a separate letter dated October 28, 2024 addresses internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance with laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements. Scope and timing followed the planning meeting of August 27, 2024. Significant accounting policies are described in Note 2; no new policies were adopted and no application changed during 2024; no transactions lacked authoritative guidance; no transactions were recognized in a different period than when they occurred. The most sensitive estimates were the District's share of the MPSERS net pension liability and the OPEB net asset recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75, estimated as of June 30, 2024 at $288.9 million and $4.9 million respectively, based on data from the Office of Retirement Services. Disclosures are neutral, consistent, and clear. No significant difficulties, no disagreements with management, and management corrected all known and likely misstatements other than trivial ones. Management representations are in the letter dated October 28, 2024. There were no consultations with other independent accountants, and nothing in the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report appeared materially misstated or inconsistent.

OTHER RECOMMENDATIONS AND OBSERVATIONS. Food Service Fund - Fund Balance: the fund balance continues to exceed the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures; the District should continue to monitor its spenddown plan entered into with the Michigan Department of Education to reduce the balance to an acceptable level. The same item is repeated in the Informational Items section.

SCHOOL AID, 2023/2024. The May 2023 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference identified significant new resources. The target foundation allowance rose $458 per pupil to $9,608, a 5 percent increase; hold harmless districts also received the $458 increase; cyber schools received no increase and continued at $9,150. The blended pupil count continued at 90 percent weighting for the October 2023 count and 10 percent for the February 2023 count, with a two-year blend for declining enrollment districts whose 2023 final membership count was lower than the 2022 final count, funded through Section 29. Special education funding became fully categorical from Section 51 of the State Aid Act rather than partly from Section 20, and no longer supplements Headlee Amendment payments from the foundation allowance. The MPSERS overall contribution rate increased to 48 percent of payroll from 45 percent, with the District's net cost rising from 28 percent to approximately 31 percent, the first such increase in several years. GSRP reimbursement was funded at the target foundation allowance level with higher income limits; Section 31a/At-Risk funding increased using an opportunity index; Section 30d provided universal free breakfast and lunch, state funded and not replacing the federal Child Nutrition Cluster; transportation funding used a riders-per-square-mile formula; one-time funds supported mental health and school safety and a student loan repayment program, funded late in the year and creating revenue recognition challenges at June 30, 2024; and ISD operations funding rose 5 percent.

SCHOOL AID, 2024/2025. The May 2024 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference predicted sufficient resources for current programs but slower growth, closer to pre-pandemic levels. The enacted bill provided no foundation allowance increase, holding the target at $9,608 per pupil; instead modifications, primarily to retirement funding, free up about $400 per pupil for operations, though not every district realizes the full $400. Before the conference report, each version of the bill provided a foundation increase ranging from $217 to $302 per pupil. Declining enrollment smoothing continues; the State's Headlee obligation is funded from the special education allocation; Section 147 MPSERS categoricals were revised to increase retirement funding. OPEB is now considered fully funded; state funding covers the historical OPEB UAAL of about $669 million statewide, and the bill redirects $598 million of the savings back to districts through categorical 147a4, representing approximately 5.75 percent of MPSERS-related payroll. GSRP eligibility extends to families below four times the federal poverty level. At-risk funding is now over $1 billion with new flexibility provisions. Transportation, Future Educator Fellowship, Student Teacher Stipend, and ISD Operations support continue without substantive change; many smaller categoricals were eliminated or reduced, the most significant reduction being mental health and school safety.

LOOKING FORWARD. The May 2024 conference looked into 2025, 2026, and 2027 and indicated funding levels are leveling off. ARP ESSER III, funded under the Education Stabilization Fund, sunset September 30, 2024, creating a funding cliff. Statewide enrollment has historically been slightly under 1.5 million students; pre-pandemic annual declines ran about 10,000 students per year, while pandemic-era statewide enrollment decreased in excess of 50,000 students, with only partial recovery expected. On average it takes about 10 students to fully fund a teacher position. Listed challenges include recession impact, ESSER III utilization, staff and student retention, learning loss programs, expanded GSRP facilities, inflation and technology costs, and security and mental health staffing. The next Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference occurs in January 2025.

MICHIGAN SCHOOL MEALS. For 2023/2024 the District received $3,676,677 in state funding under Section 30d, supporting the Food Service Fund and replacing revenue previously received from student-paid meals. Districts apply through the Coordinated Application in the State's NexSys system and must participate in the National School Lunch Program, serve breakfast and lunch at no cost to pre-K through 12th grade students, adopt the Community Eligibility Provision (CEP), collect family income information, and write off outstanding student negative balances, funded from sources outside the Food Service Fund under MDE guidance.

GRANTS MANAGEMENT AND MPSERS. Title I, Special Education, and Child Nutrition, plus pandemic programs ESSER, GEER, and CRF, have increased workload and grants management risk; the auditor suggests a risk assessment of key processes and controls in fiscal year 2025. The MPSERS plan has a September 30 year end. At September 30, 2023 the pension portion had a net pension liability of approximately $32.4 billion, a decrease of approximately 15 percent from $37.9 billion at September 30, 2022, driven by net investment returns; the annual investment rate of return was 8.3 percent for the year ended September 30, 2023 compared with an investment loss of 4.8 percent for the year ended September 30, 2022. The retiree health care (OPEB) portion had a net OPEB asset of approximately $566 million at September 30, 2023 compared with a net OPEB liability of $2.1 billion at September 30, 2022.

FUND BALANCE. During 2023/2024 the District's General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $4.2 million, increasing the General Fund fund balance to approximately $36.8 million at June 30, 2024. The statewide average for school districts at June 30, 2023 was approximately 21.86 percent of expenditures and outgoing transfers, equal to about an 11-week period of operating costs. The District's fund balance percentage is 19.21 percent and equals approximately 10 weeks of operation.

UPCOMING PRONOUNCEMENTS. GASB Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences, requires a full accrual liability for leave attributable to services already rendered that accumulates and is more likely than not to be used or paid, measured at each employee's pay rate at the statement date, replacing gross additions and reductions disclosure with net change and removing the disclosure of which funds liquidate the liability; effective for the year ending June 30, 2025, including cumulative effects on net assets as of July 1, 2024. GASB Statement No. 102, Certain Risk Disclosures, effective June 30, 2025, requires disclosure of concentrations or constraints, related events, and mitigating actions. GASB Statement No. 103, Financial Reporting Model Improvements, effective June 30, 2026, revises Statement 34 reporting: MD&A limited to five topics, proprietary fund operating/nonoperating definitions with a new subtotal for operating income (loss) and noncapital subsidies, budgetary comparisons reported only in required supplementary information, separate major component unit presentation, and separate presentation of unusual or infrequent items.

SINKING FUNDS AND TREASURY GUIDANCE. Legislation effective August 6, 2023 allows a sinking fund millage approved by voters after May 7, 2023 to fund acquisition of student transportation vehicles and related parts, supplies, and equipment, and trucks and vans registered under the Michigan vehicle code, 1949 PA 300, MCL 257.1 to 257.923, used for building maintenance. Sinking funds authorized prior to March 29, 2017, between March 29, 2017 and May 7, 2023, and after May 7, 2023 must be accounted for separately, each with its own balance sheet and statement of revenue, expenditures, and changes in fund balance, and an annual independent sinking fund audit is required. Michigan Department of Treasury Numbered Letter 2023-1 supersedes Bulletin 7 and Numbered Letter 2004-4 effective for compliance audits reported for the June 30, 2024 reporting period; Plante & Moran participated in reviewing the guidance. Districts no longer submit financial information at bond closeout but must submit an annual transmittal letter on the bond-funded Capital Projects Fund; the completion date is the June 30 immediately following the later of the certificate of substantial completion or 95 percent of bond proceeds being spent; multiple series approved by electors at the same time may be accounted for in one fund; and levies renewed after May 7, 2023 must be in a capital projects fund separate from balances from levies authorized before that date.

ARBITRAGE AND OTHER ITEMS. Arbitrage is the difference between interest expense paid by the bond issuer and earnings on invested bond proceeds, with a computation generally completed at the five-year anniversary of the original bond sale for reporting excess earnings to the Internal Revenue Service. The District has unspent bond proceeds accruing investment earnings at June 30; its analysis determined an arbitrage liability of $3,693,631, reported in the government-wide statement of net position at June 30, 2024. The Inflation Reduction Act, signed August 16, 2022, allocated $369 billion over 10 years for energy and climate projects targeting roughly 40 percent emissions reduction by 2030, and offers tax-exempt entities a direct-payment option for qualifying capital improvements such as certain electric vehicles and solar panels, with many credits available through 2032. OMB's April 2024 Uniform Guidance revisions raise the single audit threshold and the Type A program threshold from $750,000 to $1 million, effective for fiscal year ends starting on or after October 1, 2024 and therefore applicable to the District's fiscal year ending June 30, 2026; the equipment capitalization threshold rises from $5,000 to $10,000, with tracking still required below that if District policy is set lower. Closing advisory items address cyber threats (citing the K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021 signed in October 2021 and PII, FERPA, HIPAA, and PCI data), operations review and controls assessment, IT assessment and planning, and data analytics.

2024_019_tsd_2425_02_roof_program_2025_c.paragraph: Contractor bid recommendation transmittal dated 11-11-24 from WeatherTech Consulting Group, Inc. to Rob Carson of Troy School District for Bid No. 2425-02, the Troy School District 2025 Roof Program, presented at the November 12, 2024 meeting. WeatherTech recommends award to Royal Roofing and to Division 7 Building Contractors following a non-mandatory pre-bid conference on 10/25/24 attended by eight bidders and nine electronic bids opened and read aloud on 11/5/24. Royal Roofing is recommended for Baker Middle School Roof Areas B, E and the Front Entrance Canopy at $607,900.00 and for Troy Union Elementary Roof Area F at $537,900.00, and Division 7 Building Contractors for the Service Building Roof Area C at $88,922.00.
